results.proposed_proof:
**Given:** Full AC, a metric space $(X,d)$, and a sheaf of abelian groups
$\mathcal F$ on $X$.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: every family of nonempty sets has a choice function; in particular metric open covers have locally finite open refinements.

[F1] [[def-metric-space]] and [[thm-stone-metric-spaces-are-paracompact]]: a metric space is Hausdorff and, under AC, every open cover has a locally finite open refinement; this is paracompactness as defined in [[def-paracompact-space]].

[F2] [[lem-paracompact-hausdorff-cover-shrinking]]: a locally finite open cover of a paracompact Hausdorff space has a locally finite shrinking with $\overline{V_i}\subset W_i\subset\overline{W_i}\subset U_i$.

[F3] [[thm-exactness-of-sheaves-stalkwise]]: a short sequence of abelian sheaves is exact exactly when it is exact on every stalk; hence an epimorphism of sheaves supplies local lifts of sections near each point.

[F4] [[def-cech-cochain-complex-open-cover]], [[def-cech-cohomology-open-cover]], and [[def-global-cech-cohomology-directed-limit]]: ordered Čech cochains are products of sections on finite intersections, their differential is the alternating restriction sum, fixed-cover cohomology is the cohomology of that complex, and $\check H^q(X,\mathcal F)$ is the directed colimit over covers with equality witnessed after a common refinement.

[F5] [[def-kernel-cokernel-image-sheaves]]: the kernel sheaf of a morphism of sheaves is computed objectwise, so sections of the middle sheaf mapping to zero lie in the first sheaf.

[F6] [[thm-abelian-sheaves-have-enough-injectives]] and [[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]: under AC every abelian sheaf embeds in an injective sheaf and $H^q(X,-)$ is the right derived functor of $\Gamma(X,-)$.

[F7] [[lem-injective-sheaves-flasque]] and [[thm-flasque-sheaves-acyclic]]: injective abelian sheaves are flasque, and every restriction of a flasque sheaf has zero positive derived global-sections cohomology.

[F8] [[thm-leray-acyclic-cover-theorem]]: if all finite intersections of an open cover are acyclic for a sheaf, fixed-cover Čech cohomology maps isomorphically to derived sheaf cohomology.

[F9] [[lem-cech-h0-global-sections]] and [[thm-zero-sheaf-cohomology-global-sections]]: fixed-cover Čech degree zero and derived sheaf cohomology degree zero are canonically $\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)$.

[F10] [[def-cohomological-delta-functor]], [[thm-right-derived-functors-form-a-cohomological-delta-functor]], and [[thm-derived-functors-are-universal-delta-functors]]: under DC, the right derived functors of the additive left exact global-sections functor form a universal cohomological delta functor; full AC supplies DC.

[F11] [[def-effaceable-cohomological-delta-functor-in-positive-degrees]] and [[thm-effaceable-cohomological-delta-functors-are-universal]]: a cohomological delta functor effaceable by injectives in positive degrees is universal; [[cor-universal-delta-functors-extending-the-same-degree-zero-functor-are-uniquely-isomorphic]] gives the unique natural isomorphism between universal delta functors extending the same degree-zero identification.

[F12] [[thm-long-exact-sequence-in-cohomology]]: a short exact sequence of cochain complexes induces a natural long exact sequence in cohomology.



**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Let $0\to\mathcal A\to\mathcal B\to\mathcal C\to0$ be a short exact sequence of abelian sheaves and let $c$ be a Čech $p$-cochain of $\mathcal C$ on an open cover $\mathcal U$. By [F1], refine $\mathcal U$ to a locally finite cover and then use [F2] to choose locally finite covers $\{V_i\}$ and $\{W_i\}$ with $\overline{V_i}\subset W_i\subset\overline{W_i}\subset U_i$. For each point $x$, local surjectivity from [F3] lifts each section $c_{i_0\ldots i_p}$ on a neighborhood of $x$ whenever $x\in U_{i_0}\cap\cdots\cap U_{i_p}$. Local finiteness leaves only finitely many $U_i$ containing $x$, finitely many such tuples, and a preliminary neighborhood $O_x$ meeting only finitely many $W_i$. For each tuple containing $x$, choose a neighborhood on which its section lifts. For the finite set of $W_i$ meeting $O_x$, shrink a neighborhood $N_x$ of $x$ inside all these lift neighborhoods, inside $U_i$ whenever $x\in U_i$, and inside $W_i$ whenever $x\in W_i$; if $x\notin U_i$, also shrink to avoid $\overline{W_i}$, which is closed and does not contain $x$ because $\overline{W_i}\subset U_i$. Then $N_x\subset U_i$ whenever $N_x\cap W_i\ne\varnothing$, and every component indexed by a tuple containing $x$ has a lift on $N_x$. Choose $\rho(x)$ with $x\in W_{\rho(x)}$. Then $N_x\subset W_{\rho(x)}\subset U_{\rho(x)}$, so $\{N_x\}$ refines $\mathcal U$. If $N_{x_0}\cap\cdots\cap N_{x_p}\ne\varnothing$, then $N_{x_0}$ meets every $W_{\rho(x_j)}$; the construction puts $N_{x_0}$ inside every $U_{\rho(x_j)}$, so $x_0$ belongs to the original intersection indexed by $\rho(x_0),\ldots,\rho(x_p)$. Its cochain component therefore has a lift on $N_{x_0}$ and hence on the full new intersection. Repeated source indices give a zero component of the alternating Čech refinement cochain, which also lifts. Thus every Čech cochain becomes liftable after refinement. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, given, construct]

2.1 Construct connecting maps on cocycles rather than taking a colimit of cochain complexes. Write $d$ for the Čech differential and $u:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B$ and $v:\mathcal B\to\mathcal C$. If $c\in C^p(\mathcal U,\mathcal C)$ is closed, step 1.1 supplies on a refinement a lift $b$ of its pullback. Since $v(db)=dc=0$, [F5] gives a unique $a\in C^{p+1}(\mathcal V,\mathcal A)$ with $u(a)=db$. Injectivity of $u$ and $d^2=0$ give $da=0$. Define $\partial[c]$ to be the refinement-limit class of $a$. Two lifts on the same cover differ by an $\mathcal A$-cochain, so their resulting $a$ differ by a coboundary. If $c$ is replaced by $c+dt$, lift $t$ after another refinement by step 1.1 and replace $b$ by $b+d\widetilde t$; the resulting $a$ is unchanged. For $p=0$ there are no negative-degree coboundaries. [F4, F5, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Independence of refinement choices requires the cochain homotopy behind [F4]. Extend ordered cochains alternatingly to all tuples, setting repeated-index components to zero. For refinement maps $r,s$ from a cover $\mathcal V$ to $\mathcal U$, put, for a degree-$p$ cochain with $p\ge1$, $$ (Hc)_{j_0\ldots j_{p-1}}=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k c_{r(j_0),\ldots,r(j_k),s(j_k),\ldots,s(j_{p-1})}|_{V_{j_0}\cap\cdots\cap V_{j_{p-1}}}, $$ and set $H=0$ on degree zero. All restrictions are defined because $V_j\subset U_{r(j)}\cap U_{s(j)}$. Expansion of the alternating differential cancels the terms omitting an index before or after the change from $r$ to $s$ in pairs; the two endpoint terms remain, giving $s^*-r^*=dH+Hd$. This identity also holds in degree zero, where $Hdc$ is the difference of the two restrictions of $c$. To compare two constructions in step 2.1, pull their lifts to a common refinement. Their images in $\mathcal C$ differ by $(s^*-r^*)c=dHc$. After lifting $Hc$ on a further refinement, the difference of the two $\mathcal B$-lifts minus the differential of that lift lies in $\mathcal A$; its differential is the difference of the two connecting cocycles. Thus both constructions define the same limit cohomology class. Common refinements also prove additivity, and lifting the images of chosen cochains proves naturality for morphisms of short exact sequences. No strictly functorial system of cochain maps on the preorder of covers is assumed. [F4, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The resulting sequence of limit cohomology groups is exact. At $\check H^p(\mathcal B)$, if a closed $b$ maps to a coboundary $dt$ after refinement, lift $t$ by step 1.1 and replace $b$ by $b-d\widetilde t$; this is a closed $\mathcal A$-cochain representing a preimage. In degree zero a zero image already lies in $\mathcal A$ by [F5]. At $\check H^p(\mathcal C)$, if the connecting cocycle $a$ of step 2.1 becomes $de$, replace its lift $b$ by $b-u(e)$; it is now closed and maps to $c$. Conversely a closed lift has zero connecting class. At $\check H^{p+1}(\mathcal A)$, if a closed $a$ maps to a coboundary $db$ after refinement, then $v(b)$ is closed and its connecting class is $[a]$ by construction. Conversely every connecting cocycle maps to $db$. Compositions of consecutive maps vanish by the same formulas; injectivity at degree-zero global sections follows from [F5]. Equality to zero in a limit is witnessed on a common refinement by [F4], so these arguments cover every element of every kernel. Together with [F9] and the naturality in step 3.1, this makes $\check H^\bullet(X,-)$ a cohomological delta functor extending $\Gamma(X,-)$. [F4, F5, F9, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Let $\mathcal I$ be injective. By [F7] it and all its restrictions are acyclic, so every open cover is $\mathcal I$-acyclic. By [F8], $\check H^q(\mathcal U,\mathcal I)\cong H^q(X,\mathcal I)=0$ for every cover and every $q>0$. Hence $\check H^q(X,\mathcal I)=0$ for $q>0$. Since every sheaf embeds in such an $\mathcal I$ by [F6], the Čech delta functor of step 4.1 is effaceable in positive degrees. [F6, F7, F8, step 4.1]

6.1 By [F10], $H^\bullet(X,-)$ is universal, and by [F11] so is $\check H^\bullet(X,-)$. Their degree-zero identifications with $\Gamma(X,-)$ agree by [F9], so [F11] gives a unique natural isomorphism $\check H^q(X,\mathcal F)\cong H^q(X,\mathcal F)$ in every degree. The canonical fixed-cover Čech-to-derived maps are compatible with refinement by [F8]; their connecting-map compatibility is the same lift-and-differentiate construction $u(a)=db$ in step 2.1, computed in a resolution. They therefore induce a morphism of delta functors with this degree-zero identity, so universality identifies their limit with this unique isomorphism. This is the asserted canonical comparison. Full AC supplies DC for [F10] and the choices in step 1.1; no compact-support cohomology is used. [A1, F9, F10, F11, step 1.1, step 5.1] ∎

**Given:** Full AC, $m\ge1$, a nonempty open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^m$,
and an arbitrary open cover $\mathcal U$ of $\Omega$.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: every family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

[F1] [[def-metric-space]]: the Euclidean distance satisfies positivity, symmetry, and the triangle inequality.



**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For $x\in\Omega$ define $$ \delta(x):=\sup_{U\in\mathcal U}\min\{1,\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb R^m\setminus U)\},\qquad \varepsilon(x):=\min\{1,\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb R^m\setminus\Omega),\delta(x)\}. $$ The conventions $\operatorname{dist}(x,\varnothing)=+\infty$ and $\min\{1,+\infty\}=1$ cover the case $U=\mathbb R^m$ or $\Omega=\mathbb R^m$. Since $\mathcal U$ covers $\Omega$ and each $U$ is open, $\delta(x)>0$. For any nonempty closed set $E$, the triangle inequality gives $\operatorname{dist}(x,E)\le|x-y|+\operatorname{dist}(y,E)$ by taking the infimum over $E$, and interchanging $x,y$ gives the reverse bound; capping at $1$ preserves this $1$-Lipschitz estimate. The supremum of a family of $1$-Lipschitz functions is $1$-Lipschitz because $f_U(x)\le f_U(y)+|x-y|$ for every $U$, hence $\sup_Uf_U(x)\le\sup_Uf_U(y)+|x-y|$, and likewise after interchanging $x,y$. The minimum of two $1$-Lipschitz functions satisfies the same estimate, so $\varepsilon$ is $1$-Lipschitz. For each $x$, the definition of the supremum supplies $U_x\in\mathcal U$ with $\min\{1,\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb R^m\setminus U_x)\}>\delta(x)/2$, hence $B(x,\delta(x)/2)\subset U_x$. Also $\varepsilon(x)\le\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb R^m\setminus\Omega)$. [A1, F1, given, construct]

2.1 Let $\mathcal Q$ be the family of all closed dyadic cubes $Q\subset\Omega$ satisfying $$\operatorname{diam}(Q)<\frac1{16}\inf_{y\in Q}\varepsilon(y).$$ Every point of $\Omega$ belongs to such a cube at sufficiently fine dyadic scale, because $\varepsilon$ is continuous and positive there. Each qualifying cube has diameter $<1/16$, so along the nested dyadic ancestors of any such cube only finitely many can qualify; choose a maximal qualifying ancestor. The maximal cubes cover $\Omega$ and have pairwise disjoint interiors, since two dyadic cubes with intersecting interiors are nested and a contained qualifying cube cannot be maximal. [step 1.1, construct]

2.2 The maximal cubes are locally finite. Fix $x\in\Omega$, put $a=\varepsilon(x)>0$, and choose $r=a/8$. If a maximal cube $Q$ meets $B(x,r)$ and has side length $s<a/(512\sqrt m)$, its dyadic parent $P$ has diameter $2\sqrt m\,s<a/256$. Every $y\in P$ then satisfies $|y-x|<a/8+a/256<a/4$, so $P\subset\Omega$ and the Lipschitz bound gives $\varepsilon(y)>3a/4$ on $P$. Thus $\operatorname{diam}(P)<a/256<(3a/4)/16\le\inf_P\varepsilon/16$, so $P$ also qualifies, contradicting maximality of $Q$. Hence each maximal cube meeting $B(x,r)$ has side at least $a/(512\sqrt m)$. All such cubes lie in the bounded set $B(x,r+1/16)$ and their centers are separated by at least this lower bound in the maximum norm, because their interiors are disjoint axis-parallel dyadic cubes. A bounded Euclidean box contains only finitely many points with a fixed positive separation, so only finitely many such cubes meet $B(x,r)$. [step 1.1, F1, algebra]

3.1 We construct a compatible triangulation, allowing subdivision of faces; maximal cubes of different sizes need not initially meet along whole faces. First note that touching maximal cubes have side lengths differing by at most a factor of two. Indeed, let $z\in Q\cap R$, let their sides be $S\ge s$, and let $P$ be the dyadic parent of $R$. The qualification of $Q$ gives $\varepsilon(z)>16\sqrt m S$. Since every point of $P$ is at distance at most $2\sqrt m s$ from $z$, the Lipschitz and boundary-distance bounds put $P$ inside $\Omega$ and give $\inf_P\varepsilon\ge\varepsilon(z)-2\sqrt m s$. Maximality of $R$ makes its parent fail the diameter inequality, whence $2\sqrt m s\ge(\varepsilon(z)-2\sqrt m s)/16>\sqrt m S-\sqrt m s/8$, so $S<17s/8$. The dyadic ratio is therefore at most two. Subdivide common cube boundaries into their dyadic face pieces: on a face, record the faces of all cubes touching it, and split along their boundary pieces; on its proper subfaces use the same recorded intersections. These are finite rectangular subdivisions locally, since only finitely many cubes touch any compact cube by step 2.2. Compatibility can be seen one coordinate at a time: two collinear dyadic intervals are nested or have disjoint interiors, so every overlap is the smaller interval; in a face, the products of the resulting intervals give its pieces, and restriction to a shared boundary gives exactly the same intersections from either incident cube. Whenever a face is already covered by smaller coplanar faces, use those pieces, rather than retaining the larger face as a cell. Boundary pieces may further subdivide a larger cell's proper faces; that cell itself is retained with this subdivided boundary. Thus the pieces form a locally finite cubical cell decomposition whose closed cells are convex cubes or rectangles and whose intersections are unions of common boundary pieces. Triangulate its boundary pieces inductively by dimension, choosing the center of each positive-dimensional cell and coning it to its already triangulated boundary. In dimension one this simply joins successive boundary points; at every higher dimension convexity makes the cones cover the cell, and distinct cones meet only along their common triangulated boundary cones. Use a single center and boundary triangulation for each shared cell. Finally cone each maximal cube from its center to its triangulated boundary. This gives a locally finite triangulation of $\Omega$ of dimension at most $m$, with every simplex contained in a maximal cube. No infinite hyperplane is extended across unrelated cubes and no finite compact subcomplex is substituted for $\Omega$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, construct, algebra]

4.1 For each vertex $v$ of this triangulation, let $\operatorname{st}(v)$ be the union of the relative interiors of simplices containing $v$. In the geometric realization it is the set where the barycentric coordinate of $v$ is positive, hence it is open. Every point lies in the star of each vertex of its unique minimal simplex, so these stars cover $\Omega$. If a point lies in the stars of $v_0,\ldots,v_k$, all these vertices have positive coordinates in the same minimal simplex. Its dimension is at most $m$, so $k+1\le m+1$. A neighborhood meeting only finitely many simplices meets stars of only their finitely many vertices; hence the star cover is locally finite and has order at most $m+1$. [step 3.1]

5.1 If $y\in\operatorname{st}(v)$, then $y$ and $v$ lie in a simplex contained in a maximal cube $Q$ containing $v$. By step 2.1, $$|y-v|\le\operatorname{diam}(Q)<\varepsilon(v)/16\le\delta(v)/16<\delta(v)/2.$$ Step 1.1 supplies $U_v\in\mathcal U$ with $B(v,\delta(v)/2)\subset U_v$, so $\operatorname{st}(v)\subset U_v$. Choosing one such $U_v$ for each vertex defines a refinement map $\rho$; AC [A1] supplies these simultaneous choices. The star cover is therefore a locally finite open refinement of $\mathcal U$ with the required order. [A1, F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1] ∎

**Given:** Full AC, $m\ge1$, a nonempty Euclidean open set $\Omega\subseteq
\mathbb R^m$, and a sheaf of abelian groups $\mathcal G$ on $\Omega$.

[F1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] and [[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]: full AC is assumed, and $H^q(\Omega,\mathcal G)$ denotes the right derived global-sections cohomology.

[F2] [[def-cech-cochain-complex-open-cover]]: for an ordered open cover, $C^p$ is the product of section groups over increasing $(p+1)$-fold intersections; an empty intersection contributes the zero group.

[F3] [[def-cech-cohomology-open-cover]] and [[def-global-cech-cohomology-directed-limit]]: fixed-cover Čech cohomology is cohomology of $C^\bullet$, and the refinement-limit Čech group is the colimit over all open covers.

[F4] [[lem-qftx-gaga-euclidean-finite-order-refinement]]: every open cover of $\Omega$ has a locally finite open refinement of order at most $m+1$.

[F5] [[thm-qftx-gaga-metric-cech-derived-comparison]]: on the metric space $\Omega$, refinement-limit Čech cohomology is naturally isomorphic to derived sheaf cohomology.



**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Let $\mathcal U$ be any open cover of $\Omega$. By [F4] it has a refinement $\mathcal V$ in which every point lies in at most $m+1$ members. For $q>m$, an increasing $(q+1)$-tuple has at least $m+2$ distinct members, so its intersection is empty; therefore every factor of $C^q(\mathcal V,\mathcal G)$ is the zero group by [F2], and $\check H^q(\mathcal V,\mathcal G)=0$. [F2, F4, given]

2.1 Since every cover has such a refinement, the colimit over all covers in [F3] is zero in degree $q>m$: every representative becomes zero after refinement. [F3, step 1.1]

3.1 The comparison isomorphism [F5] identifies this zero colimit with $H^q(\Omega,\mathcal G)$, proving the ordinary sheaf cohomology bound. No compact-support comparison is invoked. [F1, F5, step 2.1] ∎

**Given:** Full AC, $N\ge0$, a point $x$ in an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb C^N$, and a coherent analytic module $\mathcal F$ on $U$. All cohomology below is ordinary right-derived global-sections cohomology on the indicated open set.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: every family of nonempty sets admits a choice function. This is the ambient axiom used by the sheaf-theoretic supplier theorems.

[F1] [[def-qftx-analytic-coherent-module]]: coherence means local finite type together with local finite type of the kernels of all finite-rank free module maps into the sheaf.

[F2] [[thm-qftx-gaga-analytic-oka-coherence]]: under full AC, the holomorphic structure sheaf on a finite-dimensional complex manifold is coherent; coherent analytic modules are closed under kernels, cokernels and finite extensions. For every coherent module, point and finite integer $\ell\ge0$, there is a chart neighborhood with a partial finite-rank free resolution exact at the module and at every free term except possibly the leftmost. No global free resolution is asserted.

[F3] [[thm-dolbeault-lemma-polydisc]]: the smooth Dolbeault sequence is locally exact on a polydisc, hence is an exact resolution of the holomorphic function sheaf there.

[F4] [[thm-smooth-function-module-sheaves-are-acyclic]]: sheaves of modules over the smooth-function sheaf on a smooth manifold are acyclic for global sections.

[F5] [[thm-acyclic-resolution-theorem-for-right-derived-functors]]: a sheaf resolution by acyclic sheaves computes the right-derived functors of global sections by its global-section complex.

[F6] [[thm-dolbeault-cohomology-polydisc-vanishes-positive-q]]: on every coordinate polydisc in $\mathbb C^N$ with $N\ge1$, every smooth $\bar\partial$-closed $(0,q)$-form is $\bar\partial$-exact for $1\le q\le N$. This is a statement about the global Dolbeault complex; its identification with sheaf cohomology is established in step 1.3.

[F7] [[thm-abelian-sheaves-have-enough-injectives]] and [[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]: abelian sheaves admit injective resolutions, and $H^q(D,-)$ denotes the right-derived functors of global sections. Finite direct sums of acyclic sheaves are acyclic, since finite direct sums of injective resolutions remain injective and global sections and cohomology commute with finite direct sums.

[F8] [[thm-exactness-of-sheaves-stalkwise]]: exactness of a sequence of sheaves is equivalent to exactness on every stalk; restriction to an open subset preserves a short exact sequence.

[F9] [[thm-long-exact-sequence-sheaf-cohomology]]: every short exact sequence of sheaves induces the natural long exact sequence in derived sheaf cohomology.

[F10] [[lem-qftx-gaga-euclidean-sheaf-cohomological-dimension]]: if $D$ is a nonempty open subset of $\mathbb R^{2N}$ and $\mathcal G$ is any sheaf of abelian groups on $D$, then $H^r(D,\mathcal G)=0$ for $r>2N$.



**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 If $N=0$, the chart neighborhood is the one-point space. Coherence makes the stalk a finitely generated $\mathbb C$-vector space, hence finite dimensional; choose a basis to identify $\mathcal F$ with a finite-rank free module on that point. Global sections on a point are the identity functor on abelian groups, so they are exact and have zero higher derived functors by [F7]. The Dolbeault complex consists only of degree-zero sections, and the isomorphism $\mathcal O^{p_0}\to\mathcal F$ preceded by the zero free module gives a partial free presentation with $\ell=1>2N=0$, exact at the required terms. [A1, F1, F7, given, algebra]

1.2 Suppose $N\ge1$. Apply [F2] with $\ell=2N+1$ and choose a coordinate polydisc $W$ about $x$ inside its chart neighborhood and $U$. Restrict the partial resolution to $W$. Write $K_0=\mathcal F|_W$ and, successively, let $K_{j+1}$ be the kernel of the induced surjection $\mathcal O_W^{p_j}\twoheadrightarrow K_j$ for $0\le j<\ell$. Exactness of the partial resolution gives these surjections; [F2] makes every $K_{j+1}$ coherent. Thus each sequence $$0\longrightarrow K_{j+1}\longrightarrow\mathcal O_W^{p_j} \longrightarrow K_j\longrightarrow0$$ is short exact. The last kernel is the image of the leftmost map; no injectivity at that leftmost free term is needed. [F1, F2, given, construct]

1.3 Let $D\subseteq W$ be a nonempty coordinate polydisc. By [F3], the smooth Dolbeault sequence on $D$ is an exact resolution of $\mathcal O_D$. Its terms are modules over the sheaf of smooth functions, so [F4] makes them acyclic; [F5] therefore identifies $H^q(D,\mathcal O_D)$ with the cohomology of the displayed global Dolbeault complex. By [F6] that global complex has zero cohomology in degrees $1\le q\le N$, and it is zero in degrees $q>N$. Hence $H^q(D,\mathcal O_D)=0$ for every $q>0$. [F3, F4, F5, F6, given]

2.1 For each finite rank $p_j$, the restriction $\mathcal O_D^{p_j}$ is acyclic: step 1.3 gives acyclicity of each copy of $\mathcal O_D$, and [F7] gives additivity for the finite direct sum. Restricting the short exact sequences of step 1.2 to $D$ preserves exactness by [F8]. [F7, F8, step 1.2, step 1.3]

3.1 Fix $q>0$. In the long exact sequence of each restricted short exact sequence, the groups $H^q(D,\mathcal O_D^{p_j})$ and $H^{q+1}(D,\mathcal O_D^{p_j})$ vanish by step 2.1. Exactness from [F9] therefore makes the connecting homomorphism $$H^q(D,K_j|_D)\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }H^{q+1}(D,K_{j+1}|_D)$$ an isomorphism. Composing for $j=0,\ldots,\ell-1$ yields $$H^q(D,\mathcal F|_D)\cong H^{q+\ell}(D,K_\ell|_D).$$ [F9, step 2.1, given, algebra]

4.1 Since $D$ is open in $\mathbb R^{2N}$ and $q+\ell\ge1+(2N+1)>2N$, [F10] makes the right-hand group in step 3.1 zero. Hence $H^q(D,\mathcal F|_D)=0$. The same $W$ works for every such $D$ and every $q>0$, because the partial resolution is fixed on $W$ and the scalar and dimension bounds apply to every open subpolydisc. [F10, step 3.1] ∎

**Given:** Full AC, a polydisc $D\subseteq W\subset\mathbb C^N$ with $N\ge1$ and $0\in D$, and the ideal sheaf generated by the coordinate functions.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: full AC is assumed, as in the local coherent-acyclicity theorem.

[F1] [[def-qftx-analytic-coherent-module]]: a coherent module is locally of finite type and has locally finite-type kernels for maps from finite-rank free modules.

[F2] [[thm-qftx-gaga-analytic-oka-coherence]]: under full AC, $\mathcal O_D$ is coherent, finite-rank free analytic modules are coherent, and cokernels of morphisms of coherent analytic modules are coherent.

[F3] [[thm-power-series-expansion-in-several-complex-variables]]: a holomorphic germ at $0$ has a convergent multivariable power series on a smaller polydisc.

[F4] [[def-skyscraper-sheaf-abelian-group]]: the skyscraper sheaf $i_*\mathbb C$ has sections $\mathbb C$ on opens containing $0$ and zero on opens not containing $0$; its stalk is $\mathbb C$ at $0$ and zero away from $0$.

[F5] [[thm-sheaf-morphism-isomorphism-stalkwise]]: a morphism of sheaves is an isomorphism if its induced map on every stalk is an isomorphism.

[F6] [[thm-qftx-gaga-local-coherent-acyclicity]]: choose $W$ for the particular coherent module $\mathcal Q_U$ of this example. Then $H^q(D,\mathcal Q_U|_D)=0$ for $q>0$ on every nonempty coordinate polydisc $D\subseteq W$. This choice of $W$ depends on $\mathcal Q_U$.



**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For each $D\subseteq W$, restriction of $\mathcal Q_U$ is the cokernel of the finite free map $\mathcal O_D^{\oplus N}\to\mathcal O_D$ given by $(a_1,\ldots,a_N)\mapsto\sum_j a_jz_j$. Coherence of $\mathcal O_D$ and closure under cokernels in [F2] make $\mathcal Q$ coherent. Define evaluation $\mathcal O_D\to i_*\mathbb C$ by $f\mapsto f(0)$ on opens containing $0$ and by the unique zero section on opens disjoint from $0$. Each $z_j$ maps to zero, so the morphism factors through $\mathcal Q$. [A1, F2, F4, given, construct]

1.2 On the stalk at $0$, evaluation $\mathcal O_{D,0}\to\mathbb C$ is surjective. Its kernel consists exactly of germs with zero constant coefficient. By [F3], write such a germ as $f(z)=\sum_{\alpha\ne0}c_\alpha z^\alpha$ on a smaller polydisc. Assign each multi-index to its least $j$ with $\alpha_j>0$ and set $g_j(z)=\sum_{\alpha:\,j=\min\{k:\alpha_k>0\}}c_\alpha z^{\alpha-e_j}$. These subseries converge on every still smaller polydisc, and termwise regrouping gives $f=\sum_{j=1}^N z_jg_j$. Thus the kernel is precisely $(z_1,\ldots,z_N)\mathcal O_{D,0}$, and the quotient stalk maps isomorphically to $\mathbb C$. [F3, given, algebra]

2.1 If $y\in D$ and $y\ne0$, choose $j$ with $y_j\ne0$. The germ of $z_j$ is a unit at $y$, so the quotient stalk $\mathcal Q_y$ is zero; [F4] says the target stalk is also zero. At $0$, step 1.2 gives an isomorphism on stalks. Hence [F5] makes the induced morphism $\mathcal Q\to i_*\mathbb C$ an isomorphism. [F4, F5, step 1.2, given]

3.1 By [F4], $\Gamma(D,i_*\mathbb C)=\mathbb C$, so step 2.1 gives $\Gamma(D,\mathcal Q)\cong\mathbb C$. By step 1.1, $\mathcal Q=\mathcal Q_U|_D$; apply [F6] with the $W$ chosen for $\mathcal Q_U$ to obtain $H^q(D,\mathcal Q)=0$ for every $q>0$. [F1, F2, F4, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

**Given:** Full AC, $N\ge1$, any coordinate polydisc $D\subseteq\mathbb C^N$
containing $0$, its hyperplane section $H_D$, the closed inclusion $i$, and
$\mathcal Q=\mathcal O_D/(z_1)\mathcal O_D$.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: full AC is assumed, as in the local coherent-acyclicity theorem.

[F1] [[def-qftx-analytic-coherent-module]]: a coherent module is locally of finite type and has locally finite-type relation sheaves.

[F2] [[thm-qftx-gaga-analytic-oka-coherence]]: under full AC, $\mathcal O_D$ is coherent, finite-rank free analytic modules are coherent, and cokernels of morphisms of coherent analytic modules are coherent.

[F3] [[def-direct-image-sheaf]]: for the inclusion $i$, $(i_*\mathcal O_{H_D})(V)=\mathcal O_{H_D}(V\cap H_D)$ for each open $V\subseteq D$; its stalk is the corresponding hyperplane stalk on $H_D$ and zero off $H_D$.

[F4] [[lem-direct-image-is-sheaf]]: direct image under a continuous map sends a sheaf to a sheaf, so the restriction maps define the target sheaf in the restriction morphism.

[F5] [[thm-sheaf-morphism-isomorphism-stalkwise]]: a morphism of sheaves is an isomorphism if its induced map on every stalk is an isomorphism.

[F6] [[thm-power-series-expansion-in-several-complex-variables]] and [[cor-uniqueness-of-multivariable-power-series-coefficients]]: holomorphic germs have convergent multivariable power series with unique coefficients, so vanishing of the restriction to $z_1=0$ removes exactly the terms with zero $z_1$ exponent.

[F7] [[thm-dolbeault-lemma-polydisc]]: the smooth Dolbeault sheaf sequence is locally exact on each coordinate polydisc, and its degree-zero kernel is the holomorphic function sheaf.

[F8] [[thm-smooth-function-module-sheaves-are-acyclic]] and [[thm-acyclic-resolution-theorem-for-right-derived-functors]]: the smooth-form sheaves are acyclic for ordinary global sections, so their exact resolution computes ordinary derived sheaf cohomology.

[F9] [[thm-dolbeault-cohomology-polydisc-vanishes-positive-q]]: on an arbitrary coordinate polydisc, every smooth $\bar\partial$-closed $(0,q)$-form for $1\le q\le N$ has a global smooth $\bar\partial$ primitive. No centering at $0$ or relative compactness in another fixed polydisc is required.

[F10] [[thm-exactness-of-sheaves-stalkwise]]: a sequence of sheaves is exact if and only if its stalk sequences are exact.

[F11] [[thm-long-exact-sequence-sheaf-cohomology]] and [[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]: a short exact sequence gives the natural long exact sequence in ordinary derived sheaf cohomology, whose degree-zero terms are global sections.



**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 On $D$, multiplication by $z_1$ gives a morphism $\mathcal O_D\to\mathcal O_D$. Restriction of holomorphic functions to $H_D$ is a morphism $\mathcal O_D\to i_*\mathcal O_{H_D}$ by [F3]–[F4], and it kills the image of multiplication by $z_1$. It therefore induces a morphism $\bar r:\mathcal Q\to i_*\mathcal O_{H_D}$. The quotient is coherent by [F1] and closure under cokernels in [F2]. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, given, construct]

1.2 At a point $a=(0,a')\in H_D$, a germ $h$ holomorphic on $H_D$ extends to $\widetilde h(z_1,z')=h(z')$, so $\bar r_a$ is surjective by [F3]. If $f$ is a holomorphic germ at $a$ whose restriction to $z_1=0$ vanishes, write its convergent expansion on a smaller product polydisc as $f(z_1,a'+\zeta')=\sum_{k,\alpha'}c_{k,\alpha'}z_1^k(\zeta')^{\alpha'}$. Since the restriction is the zero germ, [F6] implies $c_{0,\alpha'}=0$ for every $\alpha'$. The series $g(z_1,a'+\zeta')=\sum_{k\ge1,\alpha'}c_{k,\alpha'}z_1^{k-1}(\zeta')^{\alpha'}$ still converges on every smaller product polydisc, because shifting each positive $z_1$ exponent down by one preserves the positive radius of convergence. Thus $g$ is holomorphic and $f=z_1g$. The kernel of restriction on this stalk is exactly $(z_1)$, so $\bar r_a$ is an isomorphism. [F3, F6, given, algebra]

1.3 On this arbitrary $D$, [F7] gives the exact smooth Dolbeault sheaf resolution of $\mathcal O_D$. Its terms are modules over smooth real-valued functions; [F8] makes them acyclic and identifies $H^q(D,\mathcal O_D)$ with the cohomology of their global complex. By [F9] that complex has zero cohomology for $1\le q\le N$, and its terms are zero above degree $N$. Hence $H^q(D,\mathcal O_D)=0$ for every $q>0$. [A1, F7, F8, F9, given]

2.1 If $a\in D\setminus H_D$, then $z_1(a)\ne0$, so the germ of $z_1$ is a unit and $\mathcal Q_a=0$. The stalk $(i_*\mathcal O_{H_D})_a$ is zero by [F3]. Together with step 1.2 this proves that $\bar r$ is an isomorphism on every stalk; [F5] gives the sheaf isomorphism. [F3, F5, step 1.2, given]

2.2 Multiplication by $z_1$ is injective on every holomorphic stalk. Away from $H_D$ it multiplies by a unit. At $a=(0,a')\in H_D$, if $z_1f=0$ as a germ, expand $f$ on a sufficiently small product polydisc about $a$ using [F6]. Multiplication shifts every $z_1$ exponent up by one; uniqueness of the power-series coefficients therefore forces all coefficients of $f$ to vanish. Thus $f=0$. By [F10] multiplication is a sheaf monomorphism; its cokernel is $\mathcal Q$ by definition, giving the stated short exact sequence on the whole $D$. [F6, F10, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 Apply [F11] to the short exact sequence of step 2.2. For $q>0$, its segment $H^q(D,\mathcal O_D)\to H^q(D,\mathcal Q)\to H^{q+1}(D,\mathcal O_D)$ has both outer groups zero by step 1.3, so $H^q(D,\mathcal Q)=0$. Its degree-zero segment also makes $\mathcal O(D)\to\Gamma(D,\mathcal Q)$ surjective with kernel $z_1\mathcal O(D)$, because $H^1(D,\mathcal O_D)=0$. Finally the sheaf isomorphism of step 2.1 and the direct-image formula [F3] give $\Gamma(D,\mathcal Q)=\Gamma(D,i_*\mathcal O_{H_D})=\mathcal O(H_D)$. Thus both the global quotient computation and all positive-degree vanishings hold for every coordinate polydisc containing $0$, using only scalar acyclicity and this multiplication sequence. [F3, F11, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 1.3, algebra] ∎
